newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila puts blame on Beijing in Spratlys row.
newsitem.headline: Manila puts blame on Beijing in Spratlys row.

text.p: The Philippines has blamed China for their latest row over alleged trespassing by armed Chinese ships in an area Manila claims in the disputed Spratly Islands.
Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said Beijing advised Manila its ships would pass through the area but only on the same day the ships were seen there.
He likened Beijing to a motorist who wanted to make a turn but signalled only when he was at the kerb.

Manila last week protested against what it said was the incursion by four Chinese naval ships into its area in the Spratlys, a cluster of tiny islands and reefs in the South China Sea with potentially rich oil and gas reserves.
Beijing says the entire area belongs to China. The islands are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
China has insisted on its right to enter the area but withdrew the ships from near two Philippine-claimed islands after Manila's protest.
"Just like driving, if you are turning you should make a signal. Otherwise, you'll get bumped at the rear," Siazon told reporters on Saturday night.
"It's like you flashed your signals while you were just a metre from the kerb. So an accident was possible."

Philippine reconnaissance planes reported sighting a hut-like structure built over a reef near one of the islands where the Chinese ships were seen. Defence officials said the hut was appparently abandoned.
Siazon said Chinese officials did not mention a hut when the Philippines ambassador in Beijing spoke to them about the ships.
"Now, whose structure is that, we don't know," Siazon said.
The Chinese embassy on Saturday defended China's right to be in the area, saying, "China has indisputable sovereignty over the Nansha Islands (Spratlys) and the adjacent waters".
It said the ships were conducting marine survey measurements and had returned to China after completing their work.
The two countries clashed over the islands in 1995 and agreed not to disturb peace in the area.
